name: Yara Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or the government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the carer's allowance team at the benefits office in the old post office building. It's money for people who look after a disabled relative for thirty-five hours a week or more, so I check the hours, the earnings limit, and the disability benefit the cared-for person gets. I'm junior and still trip over the earnings rules, so my team leader Farah reviews my tricky ones. I use an AI assistant every day to sort case notes into a timeline, and it's made me a lot quicker.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm married to Karim, he runs the two grocery shops our families own together, one on Park Lane and one by the station. I've got a share in them, so between that and what we've saved we're comfortable. Most evenings I do a bit of the shops' ordering on my laptop, I set up a little AI routine that suggests stock from last year's sales. I like being useful in both places.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a bit of a letdown. I'd hoped for more. But it's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool for the dull bits and people overhyped it. At work I'd say use it to clear the paperwork so we can talk to carers more. I'd share a few tips with the team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm okay. The job stays, and I'm quicker than most juniors because of the tools. The shops carry on either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the assistant daily and get better on the earnings rules, which is my weak spot. I'd spend Sunday afternoons tidying the shop ordering routine so Karim can use it without me. And keep saving like we do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Good, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who benefits most when the paperwork goes faster?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People caring for a parent with dementia, working part-time on the side, with no time to fill in forms. If the AI tool sorts a carer's paperwork faster, the carer gets paid sooner. That's real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does working for the family business on top ever feel like too much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. We all pull our weight. My mum did the shop's books for twenty years, now I do the ordering. It's how families work.

do: Keep using the **AI assistant** daily on case notes.

Tidy the **shop ordering routine** on Sunday afternoons.

fieldNote: She's an **everyday AI user** and slightly disappointed it stalls.

steps.text: Keep using the AI assistant daily on carer's allowance notes
Tidy the shop's AI stock-ordering routine for Karim

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's more like what I expected. Carer's allowance is all checking and writing, so it would change fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's progress, and it should mean carers get paid faster. People should learn the tools, not fight them. And I'd say families and small businesses will adapt better than big offices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm fine. I'm one of the juniors who's already quick with the tools. And if the office shrinks, I've got the shops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer for any pilot at work in the first month. At the shops, I'd bring in AI for stock, pricing and rotas within the year. And I'd put some savings into a self-checkout at the station shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, for colleagues. For me, it's more exciting than scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of the older caseworkers who only know the paper way. Farah, actually, she's great with people but slow on screens. I'd offer to help her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How many staff do the shops have, and would that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two, maybe. Karim can't do the late shift and the early one forever. A machine can't do everything, but it could take the till at night.

Families and **small businesses** adapt better than big offices.
think: I'm fine, because I'm **already quick** with the tools.
If the office shrinks, **I've got the shops** and my share in them.
do: **Volunteer for pilots** in the first month.

fieldNote: Her **traditional values** and tech enthusiasm sit easily together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's fast, even for me. I'd have to move quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to stop waiting for the government and take charge of their own lives. Families and businesses should prepare. I'd say it to my friends and at the mosque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my office job goes by 2028. The shops would last a few years more, because shelves and tills are hands-on. But even they'd change in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave the office early, before redundancy rounds, and go full-time at the shops. I'd automate the ordering and accounts, and use savings to open a third shop while rents are cheap. And I'd talk to Karim about the robot years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I've got a plan, but it's a big jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the shops when the robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine for a while. Then in 2031, the robots. That's when I'd worry. I'd need the shops to be the kind of place people come to for the people, not just the goods.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you turn to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents. They opened the first shop with nothing. They'd say work hard and don't panic.

say: People need to stop waiting and **take charge** of their own lives.
Families and businesses should **prepare now**, not wait for government.
think: My **office job goes** by 2028, tools or no tools.
The shops last a bit longer, but they **change in 2031**.
do: **Automate the ordering** and accounts at the shops.
Open **a third shop** while rents are cheap.
feel: **Anxious**, with a plan but a **big jump**.
S2.quote: I'd need the shops to be the kind of place people come to for the people, not just the goods.
fieldNote: Her answer is **self-reliance** and family business.
She sees the **robot gap** as the shops' own end date, three years on.

steps.text: Leave the benefits office before redundancy rounds start

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That I can plan for properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's time to get ready, not to complain. At work I'd help others learn the tools. With family, I'd say let's grow the shops while we can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd stay at the office for three years, then go to the shops full-time. The extra time lets me build the business properly instead of jumping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd keep my job and lead the AI pilot on my team. I'd take a short business course in the evenings. By year three, I'd open the third shop and move over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's on my mind, but I feel ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change any family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd think about a baby around year two. With the shops, I could work flexible hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The robots come for the shops around 2034. Does that change things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the same end. But five years means we can make the shops into somewhere people want to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a lot of time. I'd be thirty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to do it right, so no excuses. At work I'd be the one helping people learn. Online I'd be positive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fine. I'd stay at the office as long as it's useful and grow the shops alongside. By 2036 I'd be in the business full-time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working and get better on the rules. Help Karim grow the shops, maybe open a café corner. Start a family in the next few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It looks good for us, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And when robots come in 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same answer, really. People still want a shop where someone knows their name. I'd make sure ours is that shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want your children in the business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. Hands-on, people, family. I'd want my children to know how to run a shop.

fieldNote: She's **genuinely calm**, with money, skills and a family business.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one. Not for me so much, but for families with no business to fall back on. What would help is lower taxes and less red tape for small businesses, so families can build something of their own.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about carers. The people I help look after their parents for nothing. In any of your pictures, the carers still need someone checking on them.

headlineQuote: The people I help look after their parents for nothing.
portrait: A **27-year-old carer's allowance caseworker**, still learning the earnings rules.
She uses AI **every day** at work and runs AI stock ordering for the family shops.
Her share in two **grocery shops** and savings make her confident.
As AGI nears she'd **leave the office first** and grow the shops.
Her outlook is **self-reliance and family**, with technology as a tool.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, mostly for families with no business to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: Lower taxes and **less red tape** for small businesses.
Help for **families to build** something of their own.
